strings.name: Justin Trudeau
strings.summary: Justin Trudeau served as Canada’s 23rd prime minister from 2015 to 2025 and led the Liberal Party from 2013 to 2025. His tenure included social policy, carbon pricing and renegotiation of North American trade, alongside minority-government bargaining and conflict-of-interest controversies. After leaving office he took part in public speaking; in November 2026 he was reported to have joined Oxford’s Blavatnik School of Government.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 18 November 2026. Recent roles draw on the Canadian Press report of 7 November; actual activity is documented by Brown’s 22 September conversation. Party succession, resignation as prime minister and the end of parliamentary service are recorded separately, replacing outdated present-tense biographies.
strings.influence.rationale: As a long-serving Canadian prime minister, he shaped climate, immigration and trade policy, while his government influenced international multilateral affairs.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Ottawa on 25 December 1971 while his father, Pierre Trudeau, was prime minister. He earned a BA at McGill University in 1994 and a Bachelor of Education at the University of British Columbia in 1998, and worked as a teacher before entering politics.
strings.facts.f2.label: Different terms of public office
strings.facts.f2.value: First elected MP for Papineau on 14 October 2008, his service is recorded by the parliamentary database as ending on 27 April 2025. His premiership ran from 4 November 2015 to 14 March 2025. The two offices did not end together.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Social policy and carbon pricing
strings.highlights.h1.text: His government introduced regulated cannabis legalization, with the framework taking effect on 17 October 2018, and established federal carbon pricing. After he left office, the federal fuel charge ceased from 1 April 2025. Industrial emissions pricing is a separate system; ending the fuel charge did not end all carbon pricing.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Public discussion after office
strings.highlights.h2.text: On 22 September 2026 he spoke with Brown University’s president about Canada–US trade, AI regulation and democratic participation. This was a completed event. His policy assessments are his views, not independently verified economic forecasts or a new Canadian government position.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Appointment at Oxford announced
strings.timeline.t1.text: The Canadian Press reported on 7 November that the school had announced his appointment the previous day as a Distinguished Fellow and member of the World Leaders Circle. This academic-exchange role is distinct from a professorship or Canadian government office; specific teaching arrangements were not established.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Leaves the premiership; Carney succeeds
strings.timeline.t2.text: He submitted his resignation at Rideau Hall before Mark Carney was sworn in as prime minister. Carney’s election as Liberal leader on 9 March was a separate stage. Trudeau’s resignation as prime minister also preceded the end of his parliamentary service.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Wins another minority mandate
strings.timeline.t3.text: After the early federal election, the Liberals retained the largest number of seats but fell short of a majority, continuing the minority position they had held since 2019. Governing required support from other parties; this was neither a direct popular election of the prime minister nor a single-party majority.
strings.timeline.t4.title: CUSMA enters into force
strings.timeline.t4.text: The new Canada–US–Mexico trade agreement replaced NAFTA. Signature on 30 November 2018, amendment on 10 December 2019 and entry into force in 2020 are separate milestones. The negotiated outcome was the joint work of three governments.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Conflict-of-interest inquiry finds a section 9 breach
strings.timeline.t5.text: The Ethics Commissioner found that he sought to influence the attorney general’s decision concerning the criminal prosecution of SNC-Lavalin, breaching section 9 of the Conflict of Interest Act. Trudeau cited employment and other economic concerns. This ethics finding was not a criminal conviction of Trudeau.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Sworn in as Canada’s 23rd prime minister
strings.timeline.t6.text: After the Liberals won a Commons majority in the 19 October election, he took the oath at Rideau Hall, succeeding Stephen Harper. Election day and inauguration are distinct; the 23rd prime minister and the 29th ministry use different counts.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Elected Liberal leader
strings.timeline.t7.text: He won the party leadership election, succeeding interim leader Bob Rae. The parliamentary roles database separately dates his tenure from 15 April. This entry records the election on the 14th, not his inauguration as prime minister.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First elected to the House of Commons
strings.timeline.t8.text: Running as a Liberal, he won Montreal’s Papineau riding and was re-elected in 2011, 2015, 2019 and 2021. His earlier teaching work and his father’s premiership are separate parts of his background, not periods in which he himself held that office.
